name: Eritrea

facts.religion: Christian about half (Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant), Sunni Muslim about half

snapshot: One of the world's most closed states, ruled since 1993 by Isaias Afwerki, which cut ties with Ethiopia in October 2026 as Ethiopian troops reached its border.
culture: Eritrea's nine ethnic groups include Tigrinya-speaking highlanders and Tigre, Afar and other lowland peoples, with roughly equal Christian and Muslim populations. Asmara, built largely under Italian rule in the 1930s, is a UNESCO-listed showcase of modernist architecture, with Art Deco cinemas and cafés where espresso culture survives. Cycling is hugely popular, and Eritrean riders have competed in the Tour de France.
society: National service, meant to last 18 months, is in practice open-ended, and it drives a steady exodus of young people across deserts and the Mediterranean. There is no independent press. Mining, mainly gold and copper, is the main export earner. Families depend on remittances, and the diaspora is taxed by the state.
situation: Isaias Afwerki has ruled since independence from Ethiopia after a 30-year war. Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopia's army in Tigray in 2020 to 2022, but the alliance has collapsed. Since Ethiopia's prime minister began insisting his landlocked country needs a Red Sea port, the Eritrean port of Assab has become a flashpoint, and through 2026 analysts warned of a growing risk of war, with forces massing on both sides. In October 2026, as Ethiopian forces retook Tigray and reached the border at Zalambessa, the two countries cut diplomatic ties, and Eritrea asked the UN Security Council to act against Ethiopia. The ruling PFDJ is the only legal party.
power: A one-party state with no national elections, no functioning legislature and a 1997 constitution that was never implemented. The president rules by decree with a small circle of party and military officials.

argue: Indefinite national service that drives young people to flee
President Isaias, in power since 1993 without an election

story: Italy made Eritrea its colony in 1890; Britain took over in 1941, and in 1952 it was federated with Ethiopia, which annexed it outright ten years later. A 30-year war of independence ended in 1991 and Eritreans voted almost unanimously to separate in 1993. A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 killed 80,000. Isaias Afwerki has ruled ever since without elections or a constitution.
